initial_requirements: European businesses need a Virtual Company Dossier service that helps them prove eligibility for public procurement across national borders. Economic operators should be able to identify required evidence, obtain and validate attestations, compile them into a dossier package, and submit it to contracting authorities. Authorities need to authenticate, receive, translate, and view the package while national criteria and evidence are mapped to shared European requirements.

topics.topic_content: Economic operator roles and internal participants

slots.value: Economic operators, including an administrator role for managing the organization, users, and access rights; possibly an auditor or read-only reviewer for internal oversight; and in some cases a substitute or delegate who can act when the main coordinator is absent. The role should be given only to people who need it for their job, such as the submitting operator, the authority handling the case, and designated auditors or admins. While the dossier is being worked on, access should stay with the operator team and any delegated contributors, but once it is submitted the authority should gain the relevant view rights and the operator should lose edit rights. If it goes under audit, access should be narrowed to the audit group and the parties involved in the case, with changes logged so we can see exactly who had access and when.

topics.topic_content: Common terminology for evidence, attestations, and dossier packages

slots.key: Definitions of evidence attestation and dossier
slots.value: Evidence is the required proof; attestations are official statements or certificates from a competent body that feel more formal than a normal document; a dossier package is the compiled package submitted to contracting authorities. Day-to-day terminology also includes evidence, certificate, or supporting document for individual items, and dossier or package for the full submission. Key distinction: whether something is an original source document, a translated version, or a validated piece of evidence the authority is expected to trust.

revisions.new_value: Evidence is the required proof; attestations are obtained and validated evidence items; a dossier package is the compiled package submitted to contracting authorities

revisions.old_value: Evidence is the required proof; attestations are obtained and validated evidence items; a dossier package is the compiled package submitted to contracting authorities

Key distinction: whether something is an original source document, a translated version, or a validated piece of evidence the authority is expected to trust.

slots.key: Shared terms for national criteria and European requirements
slots.value: People often use shared labels like requirements, criteria, or conditions for both national criteria and European requirements. The European level is usually treated as the common reference, while the national level is framed as the local interpretation or implementation. Wording may change when a national rule maps to a broader European concept, especially if the local document names a specific certificate or legal basis that does not exist in the same form elsewhere.

It is also harder when the rules differ by country or procedure, or when the language is unfamiliar.

slots.key: Do not force irrelevant evidence into package
slots.value: If a particular opportunity has no requirement for a given evidence type, it should not be included just because it exists. Anything that is genuinely not applicable to the operator or not required by the authority can be left out, but the system should still record why it was excluded so the dossier remains auditable. If there is any doubt, the service should include the item or flag it for review instead of silently dropping it.

slots.key: Dossier identifier versioning and revision handling
slots.value: Use one stable dossier identifier across all revisions, plus a clear version number or revision label that increments with each change. Operators must be able to see which version is current, which version was submitted, and which earlier versions are archived for traceability. If an update occurs after validation or submission, the newer version should replace the old one as the active dossier when the change affects the contents of the submitted evidence or the eligibility status, while keeping the earlier version in the audit trail. Non-material updates, such as metadata corrections or translation improvements, can stay alongside the previous record without invalidating it. The deciding rule is whether the change would alter what the contracting authority is relying on. Revisions that change eligibility, evidence content, or the submitted package itself become the current official record; non-substantive corrections may be kept alongside earlier versions for traceability. Users must always see one clearly marked current version, with older versions retained as history and visibly labeled as superseded. The dossier ID, evidence item ID, and mapped requirement or criterion link should remain stable; status, revision/version number, submission or receipt timestamp, and package reference may change when an item is submitted, received, or moved. Superseded identifiers must not be reused and should remain traceable as prior versions.

slots.key: Authority-side failure handling for unauthenticated or unopened dossiers
slots.value: If a standardized cross-border dossier package cannot be authenticated or opened because of a trust or interoperability failure, it should not be treated as a normal successful submission. The authority should notify the authority side and place the submission into a failed technical handling state. A temporary technical failure is one where the underlying cause is clearly transient, such as a timeout, a short-lived service outage, or an expired connection that can be refreshed automatically. If the failure repeats after a small number of retries, or the error points to a structural issue like an untrusted certificate, unsupported format, or broken package integrity, it should be treated as persistent. In that case the dossier should be rejected from the automated path and sent to manual handling with the failure reason recorded.

revisions.new_value: If a standardized cross-border dossier package cannot be authenticated or opened because of a trust or interoperability failure, it should not be treated as a normal successful submission. The authority should notify the authority side and place the submission into a failed technical handling state. If the issue is a persistent trust or format problem, the dossier should be rejected and routed to an alternative manual handling path so the case does not disappear without trace.

slots.key: Dossier transmission, delivery tracking, and acknowledgment boundary
slots.value: The service should package the dossier, transmit it securely, and track delivery status including pending, failed, or acknowledged states; while transmission is still in progress the status should stay as “sending” or “pending delivery”; if it fails, it should move to a clear “failed” state with the reason if available; if the authority acknowledges it, it should become “received” or “delivered” depending on the standardized wording; if no acknowledgment comes back within the expected window, the service should allow a “timed out” or “unknown” state so users know it is unresolved; responsibility ends when the authority has received and acknowledged the dossier, while retaining traceability and status history for dispute evidence

slots.key: Sensitive attachment access and protection rules
slots.value: Sensitive attachments should only be accessible to users with a need to know. If the evidence is still usable for the procurement decision after removing the sensitive parts, redaction is preferred and the system should note that it was shared in redacted form and why. If the document must remain complete but is only meant for a restricted recipient set, extra encryption is appropriate, with the access constraint and protection level recorded. If sharing it would still expose prohibited personal, security, or commercial information even after redaction, it must be excluded entirely and the reason must state that it cannot be safely disclosed for cross-border exchange.

revisions.new_value: Sensitive attachments should only be accessible to users with a need to know. Where needed, the receiving side should see extra encryption or a redacted view. If an item is too sensitive to share, it must be excluded from the exchanged package and the reason for exclusion must be recorded.

topics.topic_content: Submission, receipt, and package status transitions

slots.value: Help the supplier package the dossier, transmit it securely, and track delivery status through pending, failed, acknowledged, sending/pending delivery, received/delivered, and timed out/unknown states; the service should validate the dossier is complete enough to submit. Responsibility ends when the authority has received and acknowledged the dossier, while traceability and status history must remain available so the supplier can prove what happened in a dispute. If a package is assembled successfully but the delivery outcome is unresolved, users must be clearly notified that the dossier exists but the authority’s receipt is not confirmed, and the status must require follow-up action such as retrying the send, checking the delivery log, or manually confirming with the authority. The system should also show when the timeout happened and whether any later acknowledgment was received. Criteria are maintained centrally with versioning so dossiers can be traced to the old or new rule set; if a previously acceptable document is affected by a rule change, the service must mark it as needing re-validation, tell the operator exactly what changed (evidence type, validity period, or acceptance rule), and recheck the dossier against current criteria before submission. If a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, so both sides can see that it is unresolved. The supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until the issue is settled. The service should retry for a limited period if the issue looks temporary or the response is incomplete because of a technical problem; if it still cannot be obtained in time, the case should be escalated for manual follow-up and the dossier held in provisional status rather than treated as complete. Alternative proof may be accepted only if the competent authority has pre-approved that substitute for the same requirement; otherwise the dossier should wait for the authority to decide. If the service supports escalation or retry, that should be treated as a tracked follow-up step rather than automatic closure. The system should preserve the status, the reason for interruption, and the history of what was sent or requested so someone can pick it up again later. Background checks should continue when the provisional status is only due to a temporary dependency, such as waiting for an external register response or a delayed validation service; they should be stopped or revisited later if the source evidence changes, the user withdraws the dossier, or the underlying data has been superseded and the result would no longer be trustworthy. The dossier should remain provisional whenever checks are not yet complete and the outcome could still affect eligibility or submission readiness. For the first delivery, the must-haves are the ability to identify required evidence, collect and validate attestations, compile them into a dossier, submit or receive that package between supplier and authority, provide basic status tracking, maintain version history, and offer enough translation or viewing support for authorities to inspect what they receive. When a dossier package is updated after validation or submission, the new revision should supersede the previous one for operational use, but the older version must remain stored as an official historical record. The system should clearly mark which revision is active and which one was valid at the time of submission, so both supplier and authority can see the timeline. Only users with the proper role should be able to view the version history, and there should be no ambiguity about the current record. If the package can’t be authenticated or opened because of trust or interoperability failure, it should go into a failed technical handling state first, with the authority notified; the submission should be held for retry only if the issue looks temporary, like a certificate or service outage, and if it is a persistent trust or format problem, it should be rejected and routed to an alternative manual handling path so the case does not disappear without trace. The current record should be the latest revision that has been accepted as valid and not withdrawn or superseded. A newer revision should supersede the previous one when it has been successfully submitted, validated, and either explicitly accepted or issued as the replacement version under the workflow rules. If the newer revision is only a draft, failed validation, or marked as supplementary rather than replacing the earlier dossier, then the earlier version should stay active.

If a package is assembled successfully but the delivery outcome is unresolved, users must be clearly notified that the dossier exists but the authority’s receipt is not confirmed, and the status must require follow-up action such as retrying the send, checking the delivery log, or manually confirming with the authority. The system should also show when the timeout happened and whether any later acknowledgment was received. Criteria are maintained centrally with versioning so dossiers can be traced to the old or new rule set; if a previously acceptable document is affected by a rule change, the service must mark it as needing re-validation, tell the operator exactly what changed (evidence type, validity period, or acceptance rule), and recheck the dossier against current criteria before submission. If a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, so both sides can see that it is unresolved. The supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until the issue is settled. The service should retry for a limited period if the issue looks temporary or the response is incomplete because of a technical problem; if it still cannot be obtained in time, the case should be escalated for manual follow-up and the dossier held in provisional status rather than treated as complete. Alternative proof may be accepted only if the competent authority has pre-approved that substitute for the same requirement; otherwise the dossier should wait for the authority to decide. If the service supports escalation or retry, that should be treated as a tracked follow-up step rather than automatic closure. The system should preserve the status, the reason for interruption, and the history of what was sent or requested so someone can pick it up again later. Background checks should continue when the provisional status is only due to a temporary dependency, such as waiting for an external register response or a delayed validation service; they should be stopped or revisited later if the source evidence changes, the user withdraws the dossier, or the underlying data has been superseded and the result would no longer be trustworthy. The dossier should remain provisional whenever checks are not yet complete and the outcome could still affect eligibility or submission readiness. For the first delivery, the must-haves are the ability to identify required evidence, collect and validate attestations, compile them into a dossier, submit or receive that package between supplier and authority, provide basic status tracking, maintain version history, and offer enough translation or viewing support for authorities to inspect what they receive.

slots.value: Normally only the original submitter or their delegated operator should initiate withdrawal because they own the evidence package. If the authority detects an issue, it may request or trigger the correction workflow, but it should not silently withdraw the submitter’s revision unless the national process explicitly allows that. Any such action should notify the other side immediately, and if the case is already decided, the correction should usually require logged approval from both the initiating party and the authority handling the dossier.

slots.value: The dossier and each evidence item should have stable unique identifiers that remain unchanged across submission, receipt, and package moves, especially the dossier ID, evidence item ID, and the link to the mapped requirement or criterion. At each step, the status, revision or version number, submission or receipt timestamp, and any package reference should be updated as needed. If something is superseded, the old identifier should not be reused; it must remain traceable as the prior version so it is clear which evidence satisfied which requirement at which point in time.

topics.topic_content: Error and exception handling during dossier exchange

slots.value: Service downtime, unreliable delivery, and uncertainty about whether a dossier has been successfully sent; when a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, so both sides can see that it is unresolved. The dossier should only be treated as officially received when the authority has actually acknowledged it.

slots.value: Keep the dossier in a pending state, show the supplier it has not been accepted yet, and retry or resume without losing the evidence package. If a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until the issue is settled; escalation or retry would be useful as a tracked follow-up step rather than an automatic closure. At minimum, the system should preserve the status, the reason for interruption, and the history of what was sent or requested so someone can pick it up again later. Retries are needed for reliability, but the retry window must be balanced against failing fast and telling the supplier to intervene manually. It should stop retrying once the failure is clearly not temporary, such as a validation rejection, a format problem, an authorization issue, or repeated timeouts beyond a defined threshold; at that point it should fail fast, surface the reason clearly, and require manual intervention because automatic retry would just waste time and hide the real problem. If authentication or opening fails due to trust or interoperability issues, place the package in a failed technical handling state first; retry only when the issue appears temporary (for example, a certificate or service outage), but if the trust or format problem is persistent, reject it and route it to an alternative manual handling path so the case does not disappear without trace. A temporary technical failure is one where the underlying cause is clearly transient, such as a timeout, a short-lived service outage, or an expired connection that can be refreshed automatically; if the failure repeats after a small number of retries, or the error points to a structural issue like an untrusted certificate, unsupported format, or broken package integrity, it is persistent and should be rejected from the automated path and sent to manual handling with the failure reason recorded.

slots.value: Attestation is an official statement or certificate from a competent body; day-to-day distinctions matter between original source documents, translated versions, and validated evidence that the authority is expected to trust. When evidence comes from a different national register or authority, it can be accepted as-is only if it is from a trusted source and exactly meets the tender’s format and validity rules; if the content is right but language or structure differs, it should be translated or normalized into the common dossier format while keeping the original proof attached for traceability; if the source is too old, incomplete, or delivered through an untrusted channel, it must be rejected and replaced with a fresh document from the proper authority.

slots.value: A dossier should keep one stable dossier identifier across revisions, with a clear version number or revision label that increments each time it changes. The dossier and each evidence item should also have clear labels, unique identifiers, language information, a version number, and a link back to the relevant requirement or criterion. Operators should be able to see at a glance which version is current, which version was submitted, and which earlier versions are archived for traceability. If an update occurs after validation or submission, the newer version should replace the old one as the active dossier when the change affects the contents of the submitted evidence or the eligibility status, while the earlier version remains in the audit trail; non-material updates such as metadata corrections or translation improvements may stay alongside the previous record without invalidating it. The key rule is whether the change would alter what the contracting authority is relying on. Users should always be able to see one clearly marked “current” version, with older versions retained as history and visibly labeled as superseded. If the package changes after validation or submission, the new revision should supersede the previous one for operational use, while the older version remains stored as an official historical record. The system should clearly mark which revision is active and which one was valid at the time of submission, so both supplier and authority can see the timeline. The earlier version should stay visible as a frozen historical record if it has already been received or acted on. A withdrawn revision should not disappear but should be marked as withdrawn with the reason and timestamp. If a dossier is formally canceled, the latest active revision should be closed for processing, but the history must remain intact for audit and traceability. The core identifiers should stay stable throughout, especially the dossier ID, the evidence item ID, and the link to the mapped requirement or criterion. What should change at each step is the status, the revision or version number, the submission or receipt timestamp, and any package reference if it is moved into a new package. If something is superseded, the old identifier should not be reused; it should remain traceable as the prior version so there’s no confusion about which evidence satisfied which requirement at which point in time.

slots.key: Transmission, delivery tracking, and acknowledgment boundaries
slots.value: Package the dossier, transmit it securely, track delivery status using states such as sending/pending delivery while transmission is still in progress, failed with a reason if available when transmission fails, received or delivered when the authority acknowledges it, and timed out or unknown if no acknowledgment returns within the expected window; end responsibility when the authority has received and acknowledged the dossier, while retaining traceability and status history for dispute evidence; the service can support retrieval, validation, and status tracking, but does not take over assessing the procurement case, deciding whether the supplier should win the tender, or fully handling manual follow-up with external authorities if a certificate is delayed or disputed. If a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, so both sides can see that it is unresolved; the supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until the issue is settled; escalation or retry, if supported, should be a tracked follow-up step rather than an automatic closure; at minimum, the system should preserve the status, the reason for interruption, and the history of what was sent or requested so someone can pick it up again later.

slots.value: Only users with the proper role should be able to view the version history; the role should be granted only to people who need it for their job, such as the submitting operator, the authority handling the case, and designated auditors or admins. While the dossier is being worked on, access should stay with the operator team and any delegated contributors; once it is submitted, the authority should gain the relevant view rights and the operator should lose edit rights. If it goes under audit, access should be narrowed to the audit group and the parties involved in the case, with changes logged so it is possible to see exactly who had access and when. Boundary cases should be handled separately: a delegated reviewer or temporary substitute gets time-limited access only to the specific dossier or evidence assigned to them, and an external auditor gets read-only access scoped to the audit case. Explicit assignment is required, an audit trail must be kept, and access must be automatically removed when the delegation or review period ends.

slots.key: Sensitive attachment access and protection rules
slots.value: Sensitive attachments should be restricted to users with a need to know; if the evidence is still usable for the procurement decision after removing the sensitive parts, redaction is the preferred option and the system should note that it was shared in redacted form and why. If the document must remain complete but is only meant for a restricted recipient set, extra encryption is appropriate, with the access constraint and protection level recorded. If sharing it would still expose prohibited personal, security, or commercial information even after redaction, it must be excluded entirely, and the reason should state that it cannot be safely disclosed for cross-border exchange.

revisions.new_value: Sensitive attachments should be restricted to users with a need to know; in some cases they require extra encryption or a redacted view for the receiving side. If an item is too sensitive to share, it must be excluded from the exchanged package and the reason for exclusion recorded.

topics.topic_content: Mappings between national criteria and European requirements

slots.value: National criteria and evidence are mapped to shared European requirements before submission; every package should include the operator identity, the set of required evidence items for that opportunity, and the mapping showing which evidence satisfies which criterion. During review, translated or mapped documents are used to verify compliance against local criteria and procurement requirements. In practice, people use shared labels like requirements, criteria, or conditions for both sets, with the European level treated as the common reference and the national level as the local interpretation or implementation. Wording may change when a national rule maps to a broader European concept, especially where a local document names a specific certificate or legal basis that does not exist in the same form elsewhere. There are country-specific variations, especially in how a criterion is evidenced and sometimes in the thresholds or exclusions that trigger extra documents; each country can require its own certificates, registers, or declarations, and interpretation can differ in practice. A pre-approved alternative proof is accepted only when the standard evidence is unavailable or not applicable, and the alternative has already been mapped as equivalent under the relevant national and European rules. Recognition of that equivalence is tied to the specific procurement context, since a proof valid in one country or procedure may not be valid in another. If it is in the approved mapping, the contracting authority should recognize it automatically, while the system should still show why it was accepted and who approved the equivalence. When an alternative proof is accepted under the approved mapping, the approver of that equivalence should be recorded as the authority or body that owns the mapping decision, not the operator submitting the dossier; if the equivalence comes from a national register or a predefined European mapping, the source organization and, where available, the specific official or system that issued or maintained the approval should be recorded; if it is accepted case by case, the contracting authority that approved it should be recorded as the approver.

slots.value: The service should guide operators step by step, let them reuse previously validated evidence, and flag missing or expired items so they do not have to start from scratch or rely on outside help. If there is any ambiguity, the service should indicate the document is only provisionally acceptable or needs manual review rather than letting operators assume it is fine. It should also allow items to be marked as not applicable only when the criterion genuinely does not apply to that operator or procurement case, and if the national authority does not require a proof, the exception should still be recorded for traceability instead of being omitted silently. Replacing an evidence item should be allowed only when the replacement satisfies the same shared requirement and can be mapped back to it.

slots.value: The service should show the exact criterion the document is meant to satisfy, the issuing country or authority, the validity period, and any special acceptance rules for that tender. It should also flag translation requirements, expiry dates, and whether a scanned copy, signed original, or electronic attestation is acceptable. Criteria should be maintained centrally with versioning so the service can distinguish dossiers built against old versus new versions. If a previously acceptable document is affected by a rule change, the service should mark it as needing re-validation and tell the operator exactly what changed, including whether it is the evidence type, the validity period, or the acceptance rule. A dossier should not remain approved indefinitely; it must be rechecked against the current criteria before submission. The issuing authority must be recognized, the document must be current for that opportunity, and it must satisfy the tender’s stated format and language rules.

sections.section_content: Business Rules, Regulatory Constraints, and Operating Boundaries

topics.topic_content: Procurement eligibility rules and national criteria

slots.value: In cross-border public tenders, suppliers may need to prove legal status, tax compliance, financial standing, or professional qualifications; the required evidence can be issued in the supplier's home country and accepted in the tender country. The evidence is used to demonstrate that the economic operator meets the eligibility and selection criteria for that specific procurement and is allowed to bid, and is not excluded for legal, financial, or technical reasons. Typically, they start by selecting the procurement opportunity or the authority they want to apply to, and then the service shows the relevant eligibility criteria and the evidence expected for those criteria. From there, they check what they already have on file, request any missing attestations from the right issuing bodies, and add the documents that are still valid and relevant. In practice they try to include only what supports the specific procedure, because too much extra material just slows the review down. It should show the exact criterion the document is meant to satisfy, the issuing country or authority, the validity period, and any special acceptance rules for that tender. Special handling is usually for core eligibility evidence such as company registration, tax and social security status, insolvency or bankruptcy checks, and nationally issued professional or technical certificates; each must be mapped to the tender country’s required criterion and is valid only if the issuing authority is recognized, the document is current for that opportunity, and it satisfies the tender’s stated format and language rules. If a national document does not directly match, the service should show the closest acceptable equivalent and flag any gaps or extra checks needed.

topics.topic_content: Legal and standards obligations for cross-border dossier exchange

slots.value: Must align with the PEPPOL framework and applicable EU procurement and electronic identification rules; exchange must be interoperable and trustworthy across member states, with reliable authentication and validation, and the authority must be able to receive and open dossiers from another country. The service should show the exact criterion the document is meant to satisfy, the issuing country or authority, the validity period, and any special acceptance rules for that tender. It also needs to flag translation requirements, expiry dates, and whether a scanned copy, signed original, or electronic attestation is acceptable. If there is any ambiguity, the service should tell operators that the document is only provisionally acceptable or needs manual review. Special handling is usually for core eligibility evidence such as company registration, tax and social security status, insolvency or bankruptcy checks, and professionally or technically issued national certificates; each must be mapped to the tender country’s required criterion and is valid only if the issuing authority is recognized, the document is current for that opportunity, and it satisfies the tender’s stated format and language rules. If a national document does not directly match, the service should show the closest acceptable equivalent and flag any gaps or extra checks needed. The authority should always be able to see the original evidence alongside any translation, because the original wording may be needed for legal certainty. Machine translation may be good enough for initial inspection, but if the content is ambiguous, incomplete, or legally sensitive, it should be flagged for human review. A pre-approved alternative proof should be accepted only when the required standard evidence is unavailable or not applicable, and the alternative has already been mapped as equivalent under the relevant national and European rules. It should be tied to the specific procurement context, because an alternative proof that is valid in one country or procedure may not be valid in another. The contracting authority should recognize it automatically if it is in the approved mapping, while the system should show why it was accepted and who approved that equivalence.

topics.topic_content: Operator experience for evidence discovery and dossier assembly

slots.value: Operators start by selecting the procurement opportunity or authority, then the service shows relevant eligibility criteria and the evidence expected for those criteria; they check what they already have on file, request missing attestations from the right issuing bodies, and include only valid, relevant documents to avoid slowing review. The migration is driven by the current approach being too fragmented across countries and too manual for businesses trying to reuse evidence in different tenders. The new process should help users find the right requirements faster, reuse already validated attestations where possible, and package everything so contracting authorities can understand it without chasing extra paperwork.

topics.topic_content: Authority experience for authentication, translation, and viewing

slots.value: Authorities need to authenticate, receive, translate, and view the package; the exchange must be interoperable and trustworthy across member states, and the authority side must be able to receive and open it even if the documents come from another country. Evidence often comes from different national registers or authorities with different formats, languages, and delivery times, and some attestations may be missing or need translation before submission. In practice, the authority first confirms receipt of a usable package, then procurement or case handling opens it and checks whether the required evidence is present and understandable; translated or mapped documents are used to verify compliance against local criteria, and legal or specialist reviewers may be brought in if something is unclear or exceptional. The final decision-maker is usually the designated procurement officer or the case owner for that procedure, not the specialist reviewer; specialist or legal reviewers support by interpreting evidence, translation, or national rules, but they normally do not make the final acceptance call unless the authority’s internal process explicitly delegates that authority. In day-to-day work, people usually call individual items evidence, certificate, or supporting document, and the full submission a dossier or package; attestation is used more formally for an official statement or certificate from a competent body. The key practical distinction is whether something is an original source document, a translated version, or a validated piece of evidence the authority is expected to trust. When rules or acceptance criteria differ by country, procedure, or language, the service should show the exact criterion the document is meant to satisfy, the issuing country or authority, the validity period, and any special acceptance rules for that tender. It should also flag translation requirements, expiry dates, and whether a scanned copy, signed original, or electronic attestation is acceptable. If there is any ambiguity, the service should tell them that the document is only provisionally acceptable or needs manual review rather than letting them assume it is fine. Accept it as-is only if it comes from a trusted source and meets the tender’s format and validity rules exactly; if the content is right but the language or structure differs, translate or normalize it into the common dossier format while keeping the original proof attached for traceability; if the source is too old, incomplete, or comes from an untrusted delivery channel, reject it and instruct the operator to obtain a fresh document from the proper authority. For first delivery, authorities only need enough translation or viewing support to inspect what they receive.

slots.key: Availability target for submission and review services
slots.value: Submission cannot assume a single successful send; the dossier must remain pending until the authority has actually acknowledged it and provided a clear received confirmation, so it is not treated as officially received too early. Immediate reassurance that submission was initiated is needed, but official receipt only occurs on authority acknowledgment. The service should support packaging the dossier, secure transmission, delivery-status tracking, and preserve traceability/status history so the supplier can prove what happened in a dispute. While transmission is still in progress, the status should stay as “sending” or “pending delivery”; if the authority acknowledges it, the status should become “received” or “delivered”; if it fails, it should move to “failed” with a reason if available; and a “timed out” or “unknown” state should be allowed if no acknowledgment arrives within the expected window. Users should be clearly notified that the package was assembled successfully but the delivery outcome is unresolved, and the system should show when the timeout happened and whether any later acknowledgment was received.

slots.value: If the package can’t be authenticated or opened because of a trust or interoperability failure, it should enter a failed technical handling state first, with the authority notified. The submission should be held for retry only if the issue looks temporary, like a timeout, a short-lived service outage, or an expired connection that can be refreshed automatically. slots.key: Language support and translation review for dossiers
slots.value: The authority should always be able to see the original evidence alongside any translation, because the original wording may be needed for legal certainty. The service should support the official languages relevant to the participating countries, but no fixed approved language list is defined yet. Machine translation may be good enough for initial inspection, but if the content is ambiguous, incomplete, or legally sensitive, it should be flagged for human review.

slots.key: Revision supersession and historical version retention
slots.value: The current record should be the latest revision that has been accepted as valid and not withdrawn or superseded. A newer revision should supersede the previous one when it has been successfully submitted, validated, and either explicitly accepted or issued as the replacement version under the workflow rules. If the newer revision is only a draft, failed validation, or marked as supplementary rather than replacing the earlier dossier, then the earlier version should stay active.

revisions.new_value: A new revision after validation or submission should supersede the previous one for operational use, while the older version must remain stored as an official historical record.

revisions.old_value: A new revision after validation or submission should supersede the previous one for operational use, while the older version must remain stored as an official historical record.
revisions.new_value: If a dossier revision has already been received or acted on, the earlier version must remain visible as a frozen historical record because that is the version the authority relied on. The active revision can change again only through a new submitted revision that goes through the proper validation and notification flow. If a dossier is formally canceled, the latest active revision should be closed for processing, but the history must remain intact for audit and traceability.

slots.key: Active revision marking and version-history access
slots.value: Only users with the proper role should be able to view the version history, with no ambiguity about the current record. The role should be limited to people who need it for their job, such as the submitting operator, the authority handling the case, designated auditors or admins, plus separately handled delegated reviewers or temporary substitutes with time-limited access only to the specific dossier or evidence they are assigned to, and external auditors with read-only access scoped to the audit case. Access should stay with the operator team and any delegated contributors while the dossier is being worked on, then the authority gains relevant view rights after submission and the operator loses edit rights. If the dossier goes under audit, access should be narrowed to the audit group and the parties involved in the case, and access changes should be logged so who had access and when is visible. The system should always require explicit assignment, keep an audit trail, and automatically remove access when the delegation or review period ends. Only the parties who already had legitimate case access should be able to review a frozen historical revision later, specifically the contracting authority and the submitting operator, plus auditors if the case is under audit. After cancellation, no further operational action should be allowed on the dossier except for audit, legal retention, or archival viewing if those rights exist. Separate annotations on a frozen revision should be viewable or creatable only by the contracting authority, the submitting operator, and authorized auditors, and each annotation must be timestamped and attributed. They should not normally be able to create or view annotations unless they have been explicitly granted case-level access for that dossier. For other project participants or outside counsel, access can be granted via a controlled delegation model by the authority or operator, but only for the specific case and only if it complies with national rules. Even then, access should be read-only unless there is a clear business need to annotate, and any such access must be logged.

slots.value: When an evidence item is left out because it is genuinely not applicable or not required, the system should show a clear exclusion rationale such as not applicable to the operator, not required for this opportunity, or replaced by an approved equivalent. The explanation should be visible to the supplier, the receiving authority, and audit users or administrators, and it should remain in the dossier record. A pre-approved alternative proof should be accepted only when the required standard evidence is unavailable or not applicable, and the alternative has already been mapped as equivalent under the relevant national and European rules. It should be tied to the specific procurement context, because an alternative proof that is valid in one country or procedure may not be valid in another. The contracting authority should recognize an approved mapping automatically, while the system should still show why the substitute was accepted and who approved that equivalence.

slots.key: Sensitive attachment access restrictions and protection controls
slots.value: Sensitive attachments should only be accessible to users with a need to know, and may require extra encryption or a redacted view for the receiving side. If an item is too sensitive to share, it must be excluded from the exchanged package and the reason for exclusion must be recorded. If the evidence remains usable for the procurement decision after sensitive parts are removed, redaction is preferred and the system should record that it was shared in redacted form and why. If the document must stay complete but is only meant for a restricted recipient set, extra encryption should be used and the access constraint plus protection level recorded. If sharing would still expose prohibited personal, security, or commercial information even after redaction, the item must be excluded entirely and the reason should state that it cannot be safely disclosed for cross-border exchange.

slots.value: A withdrawn revision should remain visible if it has already been received or referenced in a case, and be clearly marked as withdrawn so the history stays intact and reviewers can see what happened. If it was withdrawn before being accepted into an active package, it can be closed from further processing, but it must still be kept in the audit record and not deleted. Withdrawal metadata should include who withdrew it, when, the reason, the status it was withdrawn from, and any replacement revision if one exists. Usually only the submitting operator, or someone acting with explicit delegated authority from them, may withdraw a revision. If the revision is already under active review by the authority, withdrawal should require confirmation or approval. slots.value: When a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, so both sides can see that it is unresolved. The supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until the issue is settled. If the service supports escalation or retry, that should be handled as a tracked follow-up step rather than an automatic closure. Operationally, if the issue looks temporary or the response is incomplete because of a technical problem, the service should retry for a limited period; if it still cannot be obtained in time, the case should be escalated for manual follow-up and the dossier held in provisional status rather than treated as complete. For persistent trust or format problems in cross-border package handling, the submission should be rejected and routed to an alternative manual handling path so the case does not disappear without trace. Temporary technical failures are those with a clearly transient cause, such as a timeout, a short-lived service outage, or an expired connection that can be refreshed automatically; if the failure repeats after a small number of retries or indicates a structural issue like an untrusted certificate, unsupported format, or broken package integrity, it should be treated as persistent, rejected from the automated path, and sent to manual handling with the failure reason recorded.

slots.value: The bid or tender manager coordinates the whole dossier and ensures deadlines are met; a compliance or legal person checks that the evidence is acceptable. On the authority side, the receiving role handles intake and status, while substantive reviewers judge the evidence and decide whether it satisfies the procurement requirements; a legal or specialist reviewer may be brought in if something is unclear or exceptional. The final decision-maker is usually the designated procurement officer or the case owner for that procedure, not the specialist reviewer. The specialist or legal reviewer supports by interpreting evidence, translation, or national rules, and normally does not make the final acceptance call unless the authority’s internal process explicitly delegates that authority.

slots.value: Mandatory package inclusion should cover every evidence item tied to criteria that apply to the opportunity and are required by the authority’s rules for that procurement. When the mapping is ambiguous, the evidence item should be included by default but flagged for review rather than excluded automatically. Anything genuinely not applicable to the operator or not required by the authority can be left out, but the system must record why it was excluded so the dossier remains auditable. The exclusion rationale should be a clear reason such as not applicable to the operator, not required for this opportunity, or replaced by an approved equivalent. That explanation should be visible to the supplier, the receiving authority, and also audit users or administrators, and it should remain part of the dossier record rather than being hidden. If an item is too sensitive to share at all, it must be excluded from the exchanged package and the reason recorded.

slots.value: An alternative proof should be accepted only when the required standard evidence is unavailable or not applicable, and the alternative has already been mapped as equivalent under the relevant national and European rules; it is tied to the specific procurement context, since validity may differ by country or procedure. If it is in the approved mapping, the contracting authority should recognize it automatically, but the system should still show why it was accepted and who approved that equivalence. The approver of the equivalence should be recorded as the authority or body that owns the mapping decision, not the operator submitting the dossier. If the equivalence comes from a national register or a predefined European mapping, record that source organization and, where available, the specific official or system that issued or maintained the approval. If it is accepted case by case, record the contracting authority that approved it.

slots.key: Dossier revision supersession and historical retention
slots.value: When a revision has already been received or referenced in a case, it should remain visible but be clearly marked as withdrawn so the history stays intact and reviewers can see what happened. If it was withdrawn before it was ever accepted into an active package, it can be closed from further processing, but it must still be preserved in the audit record and not deleted. Withdrawal after a decision has been issued should only be allowed in exceptional cases, such as a clear clerical error, invalid evidence discovered after the fact, or a legally required correction. In those cases, the normal withdrawal must not erase the decision; it should trigger a formal correction or supersession workflow with authority approval and, depending on national rules, possible audit or supervisory review. The original decision and withdrawn revision must remain visible in the history, with the corrected revision linked back to them. Normally the original submitter or their delegated operator should initiate the withdrawal because they own the evidence package. If the authority detects an issue, it may request or trigger the correction workflow, but it should not silently withdraw the submitter’s revision unless national process explicitly allows it. Any such action should notify the other side immediately, and if the case is already decided, the correction should usually require logged approval from both the initiating party and the authority handling the dossier. A newer revision should supersede the previous one when it has been successfully submitted, validated, and either explicitly accepted or issued as the replacement version under the workflow rules; if the newer revision is only a draft, failed validation, or marked as supplementary rather than replacing the earlier dossier, then the earlier version should stay active.

slots.value: The system should clearly mark which revision is active and which one was valid at the time of submission so both supplier and authority can see the timeline. slots.value: Sensitive attachments may require extra encryption or a redacted view for the receiving side. If the evidence is still usable for the procurement decision after removing the sensitive parts, redaction is preferred and the system should record that it was shared in redacted form and why. If the document must remain complete but is only meant for a restricted recipient set, extra encryption should be used, with the access constraint and protection level recorded. If sharing it would still expose prohibited personal, security, or commercial information even after redaction, it must be excluded entirely and the reason should state that it cannot be safely disclosed for cross-border exchange.

topics.topic_content: Conflicts, open issues, and project risks

slots.value: Main tension between giving the supplier immediate reassurance that the submission was initiated and not marking it as completed too early; the dossier should only be treated as officially received when the authority has actually acknowledged it, to avoid ambiguity about deadlines and legal acceptance. Another conflict is how long to keep retrying versus when to fail fast and tell the supplier to intervene manually, because too much automation can hide problems and too little can make the process too fragile.

Another conflict is how long to keep retrying versus when to fail fast and tell the supplier to intervene manually, because too much automation can hide problems and too little can make the process too fragile.

slots.value: Need a way to keep the dossier in a pending state, show the supplier it has not been accepted yet, and retry or resume without losing the evidence package; authority must provide clear received confirmation before the process is considered complete. If a certificate is delayed, disputed, or incomplete, the case should stay open in the service rather than disappearing, both sides should see it as unresolved, the supplier should be able to correct or replace the evidence, and the authority should keep the request pending until settled. Any escalation or retry support should be a tracked follow-up step rather than an automatic closure; the system should preserve the status, interruption reason, and history of what was sent or requested so it can be picked up later.
